chunks: "The defining equation for a capacitor is i equals C dv over dt . The current through it is proportional to how fast the voltage across it is changing.
It falls right out of Q equals CV : current is the rate of change of charge, so i equals dQ over dt , and if C is constant that's C dv over dt .
You can flip it into integral form too: v(t) equals v(0) plus 1 over C the integral of 0 to the t i d tau .
That makes it clear the capacitor integrates current, and it has memory through its initial voltage. The equation tells you a lot of behaviour directly.
If the voltage is constant, the current is zero, so at DC steady state a capacitor is an open circuit.
If you push a constant current in, the voltage ramps linearly, like 1 milliamps into 1 microfarads giving 1 volt per millisecond.
And because an instant jump in voltage would need infinite current, capacitor voltage is continuous.
When you put it in a circuit with a resistor, KCL gives a first-order ODE, RC dv over dt plus v equals V s , which is where the exponential charging curve with time constant RC comes from."
